rv.q: It's a stunning intellectual achievement that's also a total gas, a rare breed of theater deserving of protection at all costs.
With a sensitive ear for the language of New York and a keen sense of what makes each of his characters unique, Guirgis has written a play that is as complex and wondrous as the world we inhabit.
Guirgis’ compassionate play, directed with great care by Austin Pendleton, is also wildly funny — actually more hilarious than many recent flat-out comedies — and devilishly inappropriate.

Everyone should see it anyway, to experience the pleasure of a great cast making a shrimps-and-veal meal of the incredibly rich material, even as it flips between comedy and tragedy on its way to the truth in between.
In the spate of shows that ring out Broadway in 2022, Henderson and “Between Riverside and Crazy” provide the deepest satisfaction.
Henderson's gorgeous, affecting performance that deserves a reward.
Mr. Henderson, a veteran actor and an unforgettable one, brings out every profane, funny, effervescent detail of Mr. Guirgis’s ever-lively dialogue.
He's a perfect combination of rent and controlled, and his deceptively natural star turn is the twisted, generous soul of the play.
Henderson’s Walter belongs on Broadway, and it’s a pity it took this long for the production to transfer.

Between Riverside and Crazy is a play about gentrification, police brutality, and the American dream deferred, but it's also about the small moments of grace that can emerge from the most unlikely circumstances.
There are so many reasons to admire and respect—even love—Stephen Adly Guirgis' Between Riverside and Crazy that it's almost a challenge to know where to start.
So if you haven’t yet caught up with this quintessentially New York playwright, Between Riverside and Crazy is an excellent introduction to Guirgis’ work.
Thankfully, the work could have no better driver than the amazing Henderson, who is in full control of every twist and turn.
Here is the perfect play, and one of the last Broadway openings of the year.
The tale of a proud man who grabs what life has to offer while he still can, Between Riverside and Crazy is the ideal anti-tragedy for the holiday season.

What makes ‘Between Riverside and Crazy’ resonate as more than a deliciously dark comedy is the compassion and wisdom that Stephen Adly Guirgis brings to its flawed characters, and to others who invite less sympathy.
Line by line, Between Riverside and Crazy delivers as much pleasure as any play in New York right now.
The genius of Guirgis's writing is in inclining us to stand with Pops in these moments of truth, even once he admits to some morally gray deception.

As subtle in its craft as it is blunt in its language — and performed by a first-rate cast — the play is likely to make you delight in all the New Yorkers on stage in the first act…and then force you to question your initial judgement in the second.
These actors hold you enthralled from the very first words spoken.
'Between Riverside and Crazy' is a play where everyone, is a con artist...These four gifted actors know precisely how to jockey with each. They do the playwright’s poker-game of words full justice.

That new light centers around the well-grounded Stephen McKinley Henderson (as Pops) who helms an ensemble of lying (to themselves and each other) misfits that still can charm an audience years later with their depiction of flawed humanity in all its glory.
The play could not be in better hands.
It’s just unfortunate that Guirgis’ shaggily constructed plot inspires doubts about whether a brilliant cast and brilliant writing necessarily equate to a brilliant play.
After a while, even his cantankerous comedy and silent currents of emotion can’t bring this dreary play north of a puzzled, heavy eye-lidded look.
That is the genius of Stephen McKinley Henderson and Stephen Adly Guirgis.
Stephen McKinley Henderson finally plays the leading man, presenting a master class in acting.
The play is engrossing as villainy takes over, though it still leaves you wondering about the twists and turns that run into dead ends.
Walter “Pops” Washington, a deeply human portrayal of a contemporary Everyman, is the playwright’s towering achievement.
The results in this 90-minute doc are both heartbreaking and heartwarming and a potent reminder of how theater really can change lives, particularly young ones.

cn.t: Henderson delivers a powerhouse performance in Guirgis's Pulitzer-winning dramedy, praised for its vibrant dialogue and rich characters, though some find the plot uneven and questions unanswered.

sg.ra: Multiple guides converge on Rows B to H center as the best views in Broadway's smallest house (597 seats), where the intimate scale means these seats feel closer to the stage than premium orchestra in any other Broadway theater. The Hayes-specific tradeoff: patrons repeatedly flag that the stage sits unusually high for such an intimate room, so Row A and the very front can force neck-craning — one AVFMS viewer described the Hayes stage as 'particularly high for the first couple of rows, so you'll be using your neck to look up,' and a JOB patron noted 'The stage is high so you don't see actors' feet.' Rows B-H sit far enough back to clear that stage-height issue while still letting you read facial expressions in a house this small.

sg.vl: Value sweet spot where the rake kicks in
sg.ra: Rows F-M center are consistently flagged as the value band at Hayes — priced below premium but still close in a 597-seat room. The Hayes-specific reason to favor the back half of that band (J-M) over F-I: an AVFMS reviewer explicitly observed that 'Row J in the orchestra level is where the rake of the floor starts to increase so even a short guy like me can see over someone tall.' That makes J-M the first rows where a tall head in front stops being a problem, which matters more at Hayes than at larger houses because the orchestra is 'more long than it is wide' (NYTix) and the stage height is tall, so front-orchestra sightlines are flatter than usual.

The very back row of the Hayes mezzanine sits directly against the theater's staff/operations area — a quirk specific to this post-2018-renovation layout. Multiple AVFMS reviewers independently complain the ushers or crew are audible throughout the show from Mezz Row J: one wrote 'this row butts up against the row where the theater staff sits and they chatted, loudly, throughout the show'; another said 'the ushers downstairs were loud and I could sometimes hear their murmurings'; an accessible-seat user at Mezz J-101 reported 'there's some sort of operation booth to the right of this seat and it's very loud and distracting. I could hear talking and typing throughout the entire show.' Because Hayes is the smallest house on Broadway, there's no orchestra noise to mask ambient staff chatter the way a 1,500-seat venue would — in this intimate room, the booth chatter carries.
